issues.legal_issue: The proviso concerning compensation not deposited for a majority of landholdings is connected to the provision continuing earlier acquisition proceedings and compensation rules, rather than to the provision governing lapse of acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The batch concerned the interpretation of a proviso addressing cases where compensation for a majority of landholdings had not been deposited.

A High Court had treated the proviso as qualifying the provision on continuing earlier acquisition proceedings, while a Supreme Court decision had treated it as qualifying the provision on lapse of acquisition proceedings.
A larger bench was already considering related questions about the same statutory scheme.

The Court reasoned that the proviso concerned compensation, that reading it as qualifying the lapse provision could produce inconsistent or arbitrary results, and that the legislation should be construed to further its beneficial purpose.
issues.conclusion: The Court gave reasons supporting the interpretation that the proviso qualifies the provision on continuing earlier acquisition proceedings, but, rather than finally resolving the conflict, requested that the contrary Supreme Court decision be referred to the larger bench for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 24(1)(b) and (2) of the 2013 Act, the former addresses the continuation of proceedings and compensation under the earlier acquisition law, while the latter addresses when acquisition proceedings lapse. A proviso is ordinarily read in relation to its principal provision and cannot be used to nullify that provision: Dwarka Prasad v. Dwarka Das Saraf, S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, and J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Chief Inspector of Factories and Boilers. Statutory provisions should be construed as a whole and harmoniously; where competing constructions are possible, a beneficial statute should be read to advance its purpose: Eera v. State (NCT of Delhi). The Court also considered DDA v. Sukhbir Singh, Delhi Metro Rail Corporation v. Tarun Pal Singh, and Sree Balaji Nagar Residential Assn. v. State of Tamil Nadu, noting that the latter had been upset in Indore Development Authority v. Shailendra, which was before a larger bench.

predicates.supreme_court_statutory_interpretation_p: The Supreme Court considered how a proviso in a statutory scheme governing existing proceedings should be interpreted.
predicates.proviso_addresses_majority_compensation_: The proviso concerns whether compensation has been deposited for a majority of the affected landholdings.
predicates.proposed_reading_affects_unrelated_lapse: One proposed interpretation would make the compensation-deposit circumstance affect whether proceedings lapse for reasons independent of compensation.
predicates.related_question_pending_before_larger_b: A larger bench was already considering related questions about the same statutory scheme.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court considers this kind of statutory interpretation, the proviso concerns compensation, the proposed reading affects separate lapse conditions, and a related question is pending before a larger bench, the interpretation is referred for reconsideration by that bench.
